title: GROUP BY
summary: One answer per group: per station, per bike, per day.

steps.title: One row per group
body: Teodor doesn't want one total. He wants a total **per station**. `GROUP BY` splits the rows into groups and runs the aggregates once per group:
The rule: every column in `SELECT` is either **in the GROUP BY** or **inside an aggregate**. Asking for `minutes` without an aggregate makes no sense: which ride's minutes?
> **Watch out:** SQLite and MySQL (in some modes) let you break the rule and quietly pick a value from some row. PostgreSQL and SQL Server refuse with an error. Don't rely on it.

setup: CREATE TABLE rides (id INTEGER PRIMARY KEY, bike TEXT, rider_id INTEGER, start_station TEXT, end_station TEXT, started TEXT, minutes INTEGER, fare REAL, plan TEXT, rating INTEGER);

steps.explain: Two groups. `ORDER BY plan` puts casual before member alphabetically.

steps.title: Rides per station
prompt: Return each **start_station** and how many rides began there (**rides**), **busiest first**. Break ties by station name A to Z.
Table: `rides(id, bike, rider_id, start_station, end_station, started, minutes, fare, plan, rating)`. `rating` (1 to 5) is NULL when the rider skipped the survey; `plan` is `'member'` or `'casual'`.

steps.prompt: Why does PostgreSQL reject this query?
options: `minutes` is neither grouped nor aggregated, so there is no single value per bike
You can't GROUP BY a text column
COUNT(*) is not allowed with GROUP BY
The columns are in the wrong order
steps.explain: Each bike group has several rides with different minutes. Use `SUM(minutes)`, `MAX(minutes)`, or add `minutes` to the GROUP BY.

steps.title: Hardest-working bikes
prompt: Maintenance is planned by wear. For each **bike**, return the number of rides (**rides**) and the total minutes ridden (**total_minutes**). Most total minutes first; break ties by bike A to Z.
Table: `rides(id, bike, rider_id, start_station, end_station, started, minutes, fare, plan, rating)`. `rating` (1 to 5) is NULL when the rider skipped the survey; `plan` is `'member'` or `'casual'`.
solution: SELECT bike, COUNT(*) AS rides, SUM(minutes) AS total_minutes
setup: CREATE TABLE rides (id INTEGER PRIMARY KEY, bike TEXT, rider_id INTEGER, start_station TEXT, end_station TEXT, started TEXT, minutes INTEGER, fare REAL, plan TEXT, rating INTEGER);
hints: Group by `bike` and use two aggregates.

steps.title: Grouping by more than one column
body: `GROUP BY a, b` makes one group per **combination**:
SELECT start_station, plan, COUNT(*) AS rides
You can also group by an **expression**. The first 10 characters of `started` are the date:
SELECT substr(started, 1, 10) AS day, SUM(fare) AS revenue
GROUP BY day;          -- SQLite, MySQL and PostgreSQL accept the alias here
SQL Server doesn't accept the alias in GROUP BY: repeat the expression instead (`GROUP BY substr(...)`, which is `SUBSTRING` there).

steps.prompt: Complete the query: revenue per plan per day.
code: SELECT substr(started, 1, 10) AS day, plan, __1__(fare) AS revenue

steps.title: Revenue per day
prompt: Return each **day** (the first 10 characters of `started`) with the number of rides (**rides**) and the revenue (**revenue**), in date order.
Table: `rides(id, bike, rider_id, start_station, end_station, started, minutes, fare, plan, rating)`. `rating` (1 to 5) is NULL when the rider skipped the survey; `plan` is `'member'` or `'casual'`.
solution: SELECT substr(started, 1, 10) AS day, COUNT(*) AS rides, SUM(fare) AS revenue
setup: CREATE TABLE rides (id INTEGER PRIMARY KEY, bike TEXT, rider_id INTEGER, start_station TEXT, end_station TEXT, started TEXT, minutes INTEGER, fare REAL, plan TEXT, rating INTEGER);
hints: Group by that expression (or its alias).

steps.prompt: Drag the clauses into the order SQL requires.

steps.title: Rider loyalty
prompt: For each **rider_id**, return the number of rides (**rides**), the number of **different start stations** they used (**stations**), and their total spend (**spend**). Biggest spender first; break ties by rider_id.
Table: `rides(id, bike, rider_id, start_station, end_station, started, minutes, fare, plan, rating)`. `rating` (1 to 5) is NULL when the rider skipped the survey; `plan` is `'member'` or `'casual'`.
solution: SELECT rider_id, COUNT(*) AS rides, COUNT(DISTINCT start_station) AS stations, SUM(fare) AS spend
